analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited soft money to national parties and requires pre-election TV ads to disclose their funders.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the campaign finance overhaul 59-41 on April 2, 2001, but the House sent it to three committees and never brought it up for a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would shut down 'soft money' — unlimited contributions from corporations, unions, and wealthy donors to national political parties, which the parties used to influence federal elections outside the legal limits. It would require anyone spending more than $10,000 on TV ads naming a federal candidate in the weeks before an election to disclose who funded them, and it would stop corporations and unions from paying for those ads out of general treasury funds. It also doubles the individual contribution limit to $2,000, requires broadcasters to sell candidates their lowest ad rates, tightens the ban on foreign money, and puts campaign finance reports online within 48 hours.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters gain information about who is paying for the ads flooding their screens before elections, and challengers gain an edge over incumbents financed by big donors: the soft-money pipeline is cut off, ad sponsors must be identified, broadcasters must charge candidates their lowest rates, and penalties for illegal fundraising rise. Ordinary citizens who cannot write large checks are the intended beneficiaries.

how_it_helps.text: National party committees may no longer solicit, receive, or spend money outside the limits and reporting rules of federal election law — closing the unlimited 'soft money' channel [S2, S4].
Federal candidates and officeholders may not raise soft money, and party spending on federal election activity must come from federally regulated funds [S4].

Anyone spending over $10,000 on 'electioneering communications' — broadcast ads naming a federal candidate within 60 days of a general election or 30 days of a primary — must disclose it and identify contributors of $1,000 or more [S4].
Corporations and labor unions are barred from paying for those pre-election ads out of general treasury funds [S3, S4].

Broadcasters and cable/satellite providers must charge candidates their lowest ad rate, cannot bump paid candidate ads, and face random audits of ad pricing; ad buyers' rate records must be open to public inspection [S3, S4].
The foreign-money ban is extended to donations, fundraising on federal property is made a crime with stiffer penalties, and the FEC must post campaign finance reports online within 48 hours [S3, S4].
Individual contribution limits double from $1,000 to $2,000, with indexing for inflation — a provision aimed at helping challengers keep pace with the new rules [S3, S4].

analysis.who_pays: National party committees lose their soft-money fundraising operations, and the corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals who supplied that money lose their most flexible channel of influence. Broadcasters lose premium pricing on candidate ads. Wealthy donors partly offset their loss: they can now give up to $2,000 per candidate instead of $1,000, and the aggregate limit rises to $37,500.

drawbacks.text: The bill doubles individual contribution limits from $1,000 to $2,000 and raises the aggregate limit to $37,500, which critics said would amplify the voice of the very donors the soft-money ban targets [S3, S4].

The ban on corporate and union treasury funding for ads that name a candidate in the 60/30-day window restricts paid political speech; the bill itself carries fallback definitions to be used if courts strike the core definitions as unconstitutional [S4].
Truly independent spending is not capped — the bill only requires disclosure and coordination rules — so large outside spending would remain legal under the bill as written [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: unlimited, undisclosed party money in federal elections is exchanged for slightly higher individual limits and more paperwork. The higher individual limits are a real concession to big donors, and the bill cannot stop independent spending, only name it. But the soft-money ban, funder disclosure, and lowest-rate advertising rules attack the mechanisms that made six- and seven-figure undisclosed giving routine, and the bill's own fallback provisions show its authors expected — and prepared for — court challenges rather than abandoning the restrictions.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the bill 59-41, but in the House it was split among three committees and then a subcommittee, no vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 22, 2001 by Sen. McCain and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee [S6].
On March 19, 2001 the Senate discharged the Rules Committee under a standing order and brought the bill straight to the floor by unanimous consent, bypassing committee consideration [S6].
After eight days of floor debate, the Senate passed the bill with amendments on April 2, 2001 by a vote of 59 to 41 [S6, S7].
The bill went to the House, where the Speaker referred it simultaneously to the House Administration, Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce committees, with timing left to later determination [S6].
In June 2001 it was referred to a telecommunications subcommittee; no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress, and the House never voted on it [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short run, national party committees and the corporations, unions, and wealthy donors who bankrolled them kept the unlimited soft-money channel open through the 2002 election cycle because the House never acted on this bill. The same overhaul did become law later in this Congress through the House's own companion measure, so the loss to big donors proved temporary.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 22, 2001 and led its eight days of floor debate in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Russell Feingold
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-WI); lead co-author of the McCain-Feingold reform
for.what_they_did: Co-led the bipartisan campaign finance reform effort in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under a February 6 order, discharging it from the Rules Committee and having it laid before the Senate by unanimous consent.

against.name: 38 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate Republicans voting no on final passage
against.what_they_did: Voted no when the bill passed 59-41 on April 2, 2001.

against.name: Speaker J. Dennis Hastert
against.what_they_did: Referred the Senate-passed bill to three committees at once with timing left to later determination; no House vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate vote was 59-41: 47 of 50 voting Democrats voted yes and 3 no, while only 12 of 50 voting Republicans voted yes and 38 no [S7]; the 41 cosponsors split 36 Democrats and 5 Republicans [S5].

industries.note: The bill prohibits national party committees from soliciting or spending any money outside federal limits and reporting rules, ending their soft-money fundraising operations. That revenue existed to influence elections outside rules designed to limit money's role, so its loss is the public's gain under the bill's own theory.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and wealthy households
industries.note: Wealthy donors lose the unlimited soft-money channel to parties, but gain doubled per-candidate limits ($1,000 to $2,000), a raised aggregate limit of $37,500, and inflation indexing — partially offsetting the loss in a way ordinary small donors cannot match.

Both lose the right to pay for TV ads naming a federal candidate from general treasury funds in the 60 days before general elections and 30 days before primaries. Union members and shareholders were the passive funders of this spending; the disclosure and funding rules shift it back to individuals.

Stations must sell candidate and national party ads at their lowest rate, may not preempt them, face random pricing audits, and must keep ad purchase records open to the public. Political ads are among the highest-margin inventory broadcasters sell, so rate floors cost them revenue while making ad time affordable to candidates.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt and political organizations (501(c) and 527 groups)
industries.note: Party committees are barred from funneling soft money to these groups, but 501(c)(4) organizations get a carve-out to run electioneering ads funded exclusively by individual donations. The bill cuts one undisclosed money path to outside groups while leaving another open.
